newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Bank of Israel governor proposes monetary board.
newsitem.headline: Bank of Israel governor proposes monetary board.

text.p: Bank of Israel Governor Jacob Frenkel said he favoured forming a board to oversee monetary policy and making price stability the central bank's main goal, the Bank of Israel said on Wednesday.
Speaking at a seminar on central bank reform, Frenkel also proposed granting the Bank of Israel "complete independence" to achieve price stability and improving accountability and transparency.
He said the reforms should come as a comprehensive amendment to the 1954 legislation that formed Israel's central bank and as a government initiative.
The proposals, prepared by an internal Bank of Israel committee, came as pressure mounted to amend the law in response to the controverisal, restrictive monetary policy imposed by Frenkel.
Frenkel has been attacked by the Treasury and many business leaders for causing a slowdown. Some of his critics have proposed the board as a way of restraining Frenkel's authority.

A statement from the Bank of Israel did not provide many details about the proposed board, which would take over decision-making authority on interest rates. Under the current law, the central bank's governor has sole authority.

"Forming a monetary board, chaired by the governor and composed of impartial individuals with no obligations except to the Bank of Israel should be considered, in order to strengthen the standing and ability of the governor to achieve the government's targets for price stability," the bank said.

Leo Lederman, the Bank of Israel's head of research, told the seminar the central bank should have "instrumental independence but not goal independence". He said the government must, as it does now, set an inflation target but leave implementation to the central bank.

Finance Minister Dan Meridor has criticised the Bank of Israel for giving too much weight to controlling inflation. He said because of the wave of immigration to Israel and the need to create jobs, the bank had to give more consideration to economic growth.
He called for reaching a policy agreement between the government and the central bank.
Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer, who addressed the seminar by satellite hookup, said central bank independence did not conflict with democratic government.

"It fits into a democratic system if there is enough accountability and transparency," Tietmeyer said. "There should be a clear-cut goal and a convincing strategy that should be used as the measuring point."
He said price stability should be a central bank's main goal and the credibility was its main tool in influencing the markets.
Frenkel defended his monetary policy against Meridor's criticism.
"If the finance minister has a problem with the cost...let him announce a higher inflation target or change the exchange rate regime," Frenkel said.
